props.title: Signs
props.initialSlug: A family faces alien invasion through faith and fear

sections.content: Signs represents M. Night Shyamalan at the height of his powers, masterfully blending alien invasion tropes with intimate family drama. Like his earlier The Sixth Sense (1999), Shyamalan uses genre elements to explore faith, family, and fate. The film's genius lies in its restraint - we barely see the aliens until the final act, following Alfred Hitchcock's principle that anticipation creates more terror than revelation. Mel Gibson delivers one of his most nuanced performances as a former priest who lost his faith, while Joaquin Phoenix brings unexpected humor and humanity as his younger brother.

sections.content: The early 2000s saw a revival of thoughtful alien invasion films that emphasized family dynamics over spectacle. Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) established this template, but Signs pushed further by keeping the entire story contained within one family's farm. This approach influenced later films like Arrival (2016), which similarly used alien contact as a lens to examine human relationships and communication.

Shyamalan's meticulous attention to setup and payoff makes Signs a masterclass in narrative structure. Every detail - from Mel Gibson's daughter's water glasses to his son's asthma - serves the story's conclusion. This technique influenced later horror-adjacent films like Get Out (2017) and Hereditary (2018), where seemingly minor elements carry major significance. SUBHEAD: Faith and Family in Crisis

movies.title: Contact
movies.slug: A scientist finds evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence and must navigate faith, science, and personal loss

sections.content: The film's exploration of faith loss and redemption echoes through later works like First Reformed (2017) and Midnight Mass (2021). Gibson's crisis of faith following personal tragedy creates a framework for examining how beliefs crumble and rebuild under extreme circumstances. The alien invasion serves as catalyst rather than focus - a technique later employed in films like Take Shelter (2011), where external threats mirror internal struggles.
